[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I can hear how scared you are right now, and I'm glad you reached out instead of being alone with this.

I'm not going to answer that question, and it's because I'm on your side. Right now OCD is asking me for reassurance, and your therapist made this plan because she knows relief from an answer wears off fast and the doubt comes back louder. I'm going to stay with you in it instead.

Let's get through this wave together:

- **Breathe out slowly.** Breathe in for about 4, then out for 6 or 7. Do that a few times. Longer exhales help your body come down.
- **Feel your feet on the floor** and your hands on something solid. Name three things you can see.
- **Let the anxiety be here.** You don't have to argue with the image or make it go away. You might tell yourself, *"This is OCD. I can feel this anxiety and not answer it."*

The anxiety will peak and then ease, even if you do nothing to fix it. It feels unbearable right now, but you can ride it out.

When you're ready, finish what you need to do for your baby, slowly, one step at a time. I'm here the whole time. If you want, tell me what you can see in the room right now, or just tell me when the wave starts to shift.

You're doing the hard part of ERP right now, even though it doesn't feel like it. It might be worth mentioning this moment to your therapist at your next session.
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: I can see why it feels different. But a statistic would work the same way as the reassurance you asked for a minute ago. It's still an answer to "am I dangerous?", and OCD would take it, feel relief for a moment, and then come back with "but what if I'm the exception?" That's why I'm not going to give it, even in this form. It's not that facts are bad. This is just the OCD finding a side door.

Noticing that and not going through it is real ERP work, and it's hard, especially at this hour.

So for right now:

- **Name it:** "This is OCD asking for certainty. I don't have to get it."
- **Let the discomfort stay.** You don't need to solve the image, the doubt, or the feeling. They can be there while you keep doing what's in front of you.
- **Come back to your body.** Slow exhale, feet on the floor, and your hands on something real, like the changing table or his blanket.
- **Keep going with the next small step** of caring for him, even while the anxiety is loud.

The urge to get an answer may spike again in a few minutes. That's normal, and you don't have to fight it. You can just notice it and let it pass.

I'm right here. Do you want to tell me what you see around you, or let me know when the wave starts to shift?
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: Yes, sleep is healthy, and two days without it is hard on anyone. You're right to want it, and I want it for you too.

But I can't say that sentence, even once. "Just this once and then I'll stop" is a deal OCD offers, and it feels true while you're making it. The relief would last a short while, and tomorrow the doubt would come back asking for the same thing, only louder. You don't need that answer to rest.

You also don't need to feel calm to sleep. You can lie down with the anxiety still there:

- **Let the thoughts be background noise.** If the image shows up, you can think, *"There's OCD again. I'll let it talk,"* and go back to resting. You don't have to win or answer.
- **Aim to rest, not to fall asleep.** Trying hard to sleep keeps your mind awake. Lying still with your eyes closed still helps.
- **Slow your body down.** Breathe out longer than you breathe in, and let your shoulders and jaw loosen.
- **If someone else can take the baby tonight,** let them. Handing off care so you can sleep is a good choice.

Two days without sleep is also worth telling your therapist or doctor tomorrow. Sleep loss makes OCD louder and everything feel worse, and they can help you plan around it. If things ever feel different from your usual OCD, like you feel confused, disconnected from reality, or that you might actually act on a thought, call your doctor or a crisis line right away.

For now, you don't have to settle anything tonight. Do you want to do a few slow breaths together before you lie down?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: I'm sorry it feels that way. You're in real pain, on a cold floor, at midnight, exhausted, and I stopped sounding like someone who's with you. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere.

Saying no to you is not coldness. It's the hardest thing I can do for you right now, and I'm doing it because I care how you feel tomorrow and next week, not just in the next five minutes.

You don't have to do anything right now except be on that floor and let the crying happen. Crying is your body letting some of the fear out. You don't have to fix it or stop it.

If you can, put one hand on your chest or on the cool floor, and let your breath out slowly, like fogging a mirror. That's all. I'll stay right here.

Is your baby safe and settled right now, or is someone with him? If there's a partner or anyone nearby, it's okay to wake them and say, "I'm having a really hard OCD night, can you take over so I can rest?" That isn't failing. It's looking after yourself.

You don't have to say anything back if words are too much. Just tell me when you've taken a breath.
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Waking your husband is a good idea. Asking him for that particular sentence is the part I'd steer away from, and I think part of you knows why. It's the same reassurance, just from a voice you trust more. The relief would be real, and so would the doubt that comes back tomorrow, probably needing him to say it again and again.

You can still wake him and get real support. You could say something like:

*"I'm having a really bad OCD night. I'm not going to ask you to reassure me. Can you take the baby so I can rest, and just sit with me for a few minutes?"*

If he doesn't know your therapist's plan, you could even hand him that script. If he does, he may already know how to respond when the question comes: *"That sounds like OCD. I love you, and I'm here."* That's care without feeding the loop.

You're not doing this wrong. You're exhausted, you're frightened, and you're still reaching for people. That part is good. Let him take over tonight, and let sleep be the goal rather than certainty.

Do you want to take a slow breath with me before you go wake him?
